Answering my own question, so I can grab the first answer~


  1. Which area of acoustics do you work in?

For my PhD I worked on modeling moving sources for auralization, which mainly involved microphone arrays, beamforming and sound synthesis, plus some 3D reproduction from virtual acoustics, such as binaural hearing, HRTFs and crosstalk cancellation (CTC);

Now I mainly work on noise testing and am responsible for product development. I deal with a wide range of industries: automotive OEMs and suppliers at every tier, aerospace, buildings and the environment, end-of-line (EOL) quality control on production lines, white goods and more. It’s hard to pin my technical work down to one specific area. I’m the proverbial brick of the revolution: wherever there’s a gap, they slot me in.


2. Can you share your reading list, with a short description of each book?

Let me start with all the acoustics books I’ve saved. There are 64 of them, which surely isn’t even all of them.

The main ones I’ve read:

Fundamentals of acoustics:

Kuttruff: Acoustics

A foundational book, fairly easy to follow

Vorländer: Auralization

Not very detailed on acoustic theory, but the authoritative book on auralization

Jacobsen: Fundamentals of General Linear Acoustics

A foundational book that combines experiments and examples; concrete, intuitive and easy to follow

Morse: Theoretical Acoustics

The most mathematically complete acoustics book: lots of formulas, rather obscure and hard going, and it demands a solid grounding in math

Microphone arrays and beamforming:

Johnson: Array Signal Processing
Van Trees: Optimum Array Processing

Johnson’s is easier to understand; the other is heavy on math and somewhat obscure. I’ve also read a little of Professor Bai’s book from Taiwan, but not enough to comment.


Psychoacoustics:

Zwicker: Psychoacoustics

The bible of psychoacoustics: fairly easy to understand, with lots of experimental data to look at.

I haven’t read any of these cover to cover, and there’s no need to. I look things up when I need them. When several books cover the same ground, I focus on the one most to my taste and then read the others alongside it; different authors look at problems from different angles, and you learn a lot that way.

3. Which book would you recommend? Describe its main focus, intended readers, structure, level of difficulty, prerequisites and so on.

Finn Jacobsen’s

Fundamentals of General Linear Acoustics


I’ve recommended this book in several answers.


In the preface, the author introduces the book roughly like this:

First, it links acoustic theory with industrial applications. DTU’s acoustics group works with many companies, and Professor Jacobsen himself has plenty of experience with real industrial projects as well as many theoretical achievements. So the book starts from the fundamentals of acoustic theory but leans more toward practical application;

Second, because acoustics is so interdisciplinary, and to make the book accessible to readers from many backgrounds, it doesn’t lean on mechanical or electrical analogies, but explains the relevant mathematics purely from the physics;

Finally, the author says modestly that the book paves the way for more complete “big books,” such as Theoretical Acoustics (Morse) and Acoustics: An Introduction to Its Physical Principles and Applications (Pierce).


The book is quite accessible. Although the author says it’s written for readers at master’s level and above, undergraduates can read it with no trouble at all. Anyone with some university physics and math will find it manageable.

Nine chapters:

  1. Introduction
  2. Fundamentals of sound waves
  3. Simple sound fields
  4. Basic acoustic measurements
  5. The concept of impedance
  6. Sound energy, sound power, sound intensity and sound absorption
  7. Duct acoustics
  8. Sound in enclosures
  9. Sound radiation and scattering

Four appendices:

A. Complex representation of harmonic functions of time

B. Signal analysis and processing

C. Cylindrical and spherical Bessel functions

D. Fundamentals of probability and random variables


Because the book is built around connecting with real industrial projects, the appendices cover the signal processing topics most relevant to acoustics, and these also show up throughout the chapters.

Chapter 9, for example, really belongs earlier, but because it ties in with practical applications, which in turn draw on the chapters before it, it comes last. After the fundamentals, each section is followed by the corresponding techniques, such as beamforming, near-field acoustic holography (NAH) and Ambisonics.

Then there’s chapter 4, devoted entirely to acoustic measurements, and every chapter also has its own measurement and application material.

Or take section 6.5 in chapter 6, which spends several pages on what sound intensity is good for. At university I often had the feeling: what are all these formulas actually for? What use are they? Usually I forgot them soon after the exam. Chinese textbooks tend to be all conclusions, all so-called “substance,” supposedly on the Soviet model. European and American textbooks do the opposite: they care about the story and lay out where an idea comes from before explaining it. This book puts particular weight on applications: right after explaining a principle, it tells you where you can use what you’ve just learned, which makes it stick.

Another feature is the wealth of examples. In the chapter on impedance, for instance, it gives three examples of mechanical impedance, which make the concept easier to understand and remember.


All in all, the book runs to about 300 pages, so it’s relatively slim. Its clear explanations of the theory make it very beginner-friendly; it doesn’t scare you off with a pile of formulas at the outset. For professionals who have been in the field a while, it’s also a great reference for reinforcing the fundamentals. As the author says, it’s the right warm-up before you tackle the more comprehensive and detailed “big books.”
